heath_proof: Let a rational straight line A be set out, let three numbers E, BC, CD be set out which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but let CB have to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Let it be contrived that, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH. [X. 6] Since then, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, therefore the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG. [X. 6] But the square on A is rational; therefore the square on FG is also rational; therefore FG is rational. And, since E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, therefore neither has the square on A to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG. [X. 9] Again, since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH. [X. 6] But the square on FG is rational; therefore the square on GH is also rational; therefore GH is rational. And, since BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on GH the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH. [X. 9] And both are rational; therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore FH is an apotome. [X. 73] I say next that it is also a third apotome. For since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on HG, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on HG. [V. 22] But E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on A to the square on GH the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH. [X. 9] Therefore neither of the straight lines FG, GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out. Now let the square on K be that by which the square on FG is greater than the square on GH. Since then, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as BC is to BD, so is the square on FG to the square on K. [V. 19] But BC has to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG also has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore FG is commensurable in length with K, [X. 9] and the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable with FG. And neither of the straight lines FG, GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out; therefore FH is a third apotome. [X. Deff. III. 3] Therefore the third apotome FH has been found.

10.87
**Statement:** To find the third apotome.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let three positive integers E, BC, CD be taken such that: (i) BC:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, (ii) E:BC is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, (iii) E:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, and (iv) (BC - CD):BC is a ratio of a square number to a square number. Such numbers can be found; for example, E = 3, BC = 8, CD = 6 satisfy all four conditions.

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG. Since E:BC is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, the square on A does not have to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG. [10.9]

**Step 3.** Since E:BC is a ratio of number to number, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG. [10.6] Since the square on A is rational, the square on FG is also rational. [D10.1.4] Therefore FG is rational. [D10.1.3] Since A is incommensurable in length with FG (Step 2), the line FG is rational and incommensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line A.

**Step 4.** Let it be contrived that as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH. Since BC:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, FG is incommensurable in length with GH. [10.9] But BC:CD is a ratio of number to number, so the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH. [10.6] Therefore FG and GH are commensurable in square only. Since the square on FG is rational, the square on GH is also rational, and therefore GH is rational. [D10.1.4, D10.1.3]

**Step 5.** Since as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, then ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH. [5.22] Since E:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number (condition (iii)), the square on A does not have to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH. [10.9] So GH is rational and incommensurable in length with A.

**Step 6.** Since FG and GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the difference FG - GH is an apotome. [10.73]

**Step 7.** It remains to show that the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG. Since as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, by separation of ratio, as (BC - CD) is to CD, so is (the square on FG minus the square on GH) to the square on GH. [5.17] Therefore also as BC is to (BC - CD), so is the square on FG to (the square on FG minus the square on GH). Since (BC - CD):BC is a ratio of a square number to a square number (condition (iv)), so is BC:(BC - CD). Therefore the square on FG has to the square on FG minus the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number. Let the square on FG minus the square on GH equal the square on K. Then the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio of a square number to a square number, so FG is commensurable in length with K. [10.9] Hence the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG.

**Step 8.** We have established: FG - GH is an apotome (Step 6); neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line A (Steps 3 and 5); and the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG (Step 7). By the definition of a third apotome, FG - GH is a third apotome. [D10.3.3]

**Step 9.** Therefore the third apotome has been found. Q.E.F.
